edits.english: In the explanation of the Mishna, they clarify: What are the circumstances [how exactly is it] of "under the presumption of being supervised"? And they explain: As it is taught [as it is stated in a Baraita]: If one’s donkey drivers and laborers, who were amei ha’aretz and presumed to be ritually impure, were laden with ritually pure items (wine or produce that was prepared in ritual purity), and he warns them not to touch them, but he does not know if they did so or not, even if he went away from them more than a mil — his pure items are pure, as we say that since he warned them, they are afraid of him. But if he said to them: "Go and I will come after you," so that they knew he was not going with them, then once he is out of their sight and no longer sees them — his pure items are impure.

The Rishonim found this difficult: Ostensibly, from the continuation of the passage — "But if the Jew notified him that he was going far away" — it implies that as long as the Jew did not notify the gentile, the wine is considered supervised. So what is the place for this question? From Rashi's words, it appears that the question is in a case where the Jew did not notify the gentile that he was going far away, to what extent can we consider the gentile's lack of knowledge as a reliable factor. Indeed, Tosafot explained that precisely from the precise wording of the continuation, "if the Jew notified him that he was going far away," it implies that these barrels have a special presumption of supervision, in addition to the fact that the Jew did not notify the gentile that he was going far away. The conclusion of the matter, according to the discussion in the Baraita, is that the Jew can come by a roundabout way, so that the gentile fears that the Jew might arrive at any moment (Tosafot). The Ramban has a different interpretation regarding this matter; he explains that our Mishna permitted in this case where the Jew did not notify the gentile, even with open barrels. And regarding this, the Gemara asks: How can it be said that wine is presumed to be supervised, such that the gentile does not touch it, when the gentile is carrying an open barrel of wine and the Jew does not see him? Surely the gentile can see the Jew approaching and remove his hand! To this, the answer was that there can be a presumption of supervision — by a roundabout way, where the gentile cannot see the Jew arriving.

If one’s donkey drivers and laborers were amei ha’aretz and were laden with ritually pure items and were walking in front of the owner, even if they went more than a mil ahead of the owner — these items are pure, because they are presumed to be under the owner's supervision, and the donkey drivers and laborers are afraid to touch them, saying: The owner will come now, he is right behind us. This refers, according to Rava, to a case where the owner can go by a roundabout way, so that the donkey drivers and laborers do not know when the owner will come (Kesef Mishneh). But if the owner said to them: Go, and I will come after you, then once they are out of the owner's sight, the items are impure (Rambam, Sefer Tahara, Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 13:5).

If one’s donkey drivers and laborers were unreliable with regard to ritual impurity [amei ha’aretz] and they were laden with wine or produce that was pure, and they were walking in front of the owner, even if they moved more than one mil ahead of the owner, the items are still considered pure. This is because the workers are presumed to be under the owner's supervision, and they are afraid to touch the wine or produce, thinking the owner will come upon them at any moment. This applies where the road is a roundabout one, such that they cannot know when the owner will come upon them. If the owner said to them: Go ahead and I will come behind you, the moment they are out of the owner's sight the items are rendered impure (Rambam Sefer Tahara, Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 13:5 and Kesef Mishne there).

What are the circumstances described by the phrase: Under the presumption of being supervised? As it is taught: If one’s donkey drivers, etc. - This is established as a case where the owner comes to them by a roundabout way, and here too, it is a case where the owner can come by a roundabout way. And it is a wonder: What is the question, "What are the circumstances"? Surely, from the latter clause which teaches, "But if he notified them that he was going far away," it implies that the first clause is where he did not notify them that he was going far away, and that is the presumption of supervision for him! And it can be said that, on the contrary, from the latter clause which teaches, "But if he notified them, it is forbidden," it implies that if so, the first clause, which teaches "under the presumption of being supervised," means that this supervision is more significant than merely not notifying them that he was going far away. And if it means, for example, [that he did not] notify them that he was going far away, the Mishna should have been silent about the phrase "under the presumption of being supervised," and we would have learned it from the implication of the latter clause. Rather, it certainly comes to say that even if he did not notify them that he was going far away, there is reason to be concerned about the matter, since the gentile sees the Jew moving away. And know that another presumption of supervision is needed, and the Gemara asks what it is, and answers: As it is taught, etc., for example, that the owner can come upon them by a roundabout way.

What is different in the first clause and what is different in the latter clause? - Surely, they see them touching, as it states that they were laden with ritually pure items, and these are not sealed barrels.
By purifying his donkey drivers: - That he immersed them, and their touch is ritually pure.

And they ask: What is different in the first clause [how is the beginning, in the first case, different] that if the owner went far away — his pure items are pure, and what is different in the latter clause [and how is the end different] that after the owner's eyes were out of sight — the items are impure? Rav Yitzḥak said: The first clause [at the beginning] discusses a case where the owner purified his donkey drivers and laborers for this, meaning that the owner ensured they immersed, so that they would not render the pure items impure, and therefore there is no concern about their touch.

Rashi explains: Since this is not discussing sealed barrels as in our Mishna, but rather ritually pure items (which, according to his understanding, refers to someone carrying fruits and the like), they immediately become impure through the donkey drivers, even if the owner did not notify them that he was going far away. And the Ritv'a wrote that according to Rashi's words, the question should not be understood literally, but rather in the sense: What is the reason it is permitted in the first clause? Surely it is clear that these pure items become impure. But Tosafot explained that this is not discussing fruits, but rather open barrels that contained ritually pure items. And for this reason, it is not sufficient in this case for the owner to notify them that he is going far away, as in our Mishna which deals with sealed barrels. Therefore, as soon as they are out of the owner's sight, they are forbidden, even if there was not enough time for the gentile to bore a hole, etc.

What is different in the first clause and what is different in the latter clause? - This means: In the first clause, why are his pure items not impure as in the latter clause? And if you say: Let him answer that the first clause deals with a case where he did not notify them that he was going far away, and therefore it is permitted, as it is taught: If he left it under the presumption of being supervised, it is permitted, and this is when he did not notify them that he was going far away. Rashi answered that it is not similar to our Mishna, for this Baraita deals with ritually pure items, such as fruits that he holds in his hands and touches at all times. Therefore, the Gemara asks why there is no distinction. Nevertheless, it is difficult: Let us establish it as referring to barrels, and there would be no difficulty, for 'ritually pure items' can also mean items in barrels. Furthermore, it is difficult: If it deals, as Rashi explained, then the Gemara should not have asked from the first clause to the latter clause, but rather should have asked directly from the first clause itself: What is the reason that in the first clause his pure items are pure, since he holds them and touches them, as Rashi explained? Therefore, it seems to Rabbi Yitzchak that it always deals with barrels, but with open ones that are easy to touch. For this reason, he cannot answer by saying that he did not notify them that he was going far away; nevertheless, it should be forbidden, and it is not similar to our Mishna, which permits wine when he did not notify them that he was going far away, for our Mishna deals with sealed barrels. And if you say: Let us still establish it as referring to sealed barrels, like our Mishna, and there would be no difficulty between the first and latter clauses. It can be said that the Baraita cannot be established as referring to sealed barrels, because it teaches: Once they are out of his sight, his pure items are impure. But if it were sealed barrels, we would require enough time for him to bore a hole, seal it, and for the seal to dry, even if he notified them that he was going far away, as our Mishna teaches.
About contact with another: - With another am ha'aretz who encounters him on the way and was not purified for this purpose.
Even in the first clause: - Since he went far away, there is reason to be concerned about this.

And they ask: If that is so, in the latter clause also, since the owner purified them for this purpose, why should we be concerned that they rendered the items impure? And they answer: An am ha’aretz is not punctilious about contact with another am ha'aretz. Even though they themselves were ritually pure, perhaps they encountered another am ha’aretz on the way, and the pure items were rendered impure by him, and they are not punctilious about this. And they ask: If that is so, if you are concerned about this, then let us say so even in the first clause!
When he comes to them by a roundabout way: - When the owner can come by a roundabout way, so that the gentile is afraid, thinking: 'Now he will come!'

When the owner comes to them by a roundabout way (winding), meaning the owner can come by a crooked, circuitous path, in a way that the donkey drivers and laborers cannot know from where the owner is coming, and therefore they are afraid. And they respond: If that is so, [if such a case is being discussed], then in the latter clause also, why should it not be said that they are afraid? And they respond: Since the owner said to them: "Go and I will come after you," their minds are at ease that the owner will not surprise them.

Barrels of wine that were left with a gentile are permitted if there is a roundabout way that the owner can come upon the gentile without the gentile being seen in advance, in accordance with the statement of Rava. The Rashba rules that this applies when the gentile is alone, but if there are two or more gentiles the wine is forbidden, as one of them can be on the lookout while the other tampers with the wine (Shulĥan Arukh, Yoreh De’a 129:1–2).
